standard.title: Causes and Effects of European Contact on an Asian Society
standard.description: the causes and effects of European contact, including colonialisation, on an Asian society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can describe the key features of the chosen Asian society (AC9HH9K19) and describe the effects of European imperial expansion (AC9HH9K01). They have not yet examined how European contact specifically transformed the chosen Asian society — what changed, what persisted, and what the society's internal dynamics brought to the encounter.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students identify aspects of the chosen Asian society that remained the same or changed during the period of European contact; and describe the causes and effects of European contact — including British opium trade with China, British Raj in India, or Dutch trade and colonisation in Indonesia.

nodes.label: Nature and causes of European contact — trade, competition and control
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how European contact with the chosen Asian society developed — from trade to colonisation — and explain the European motivations driving increasing engagement.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe how European contact developed over time (from trade to greater control) and identify at least two motivations driving European engagement.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the development of contact — the East India Companies as commercial and then political actors; European competition for trade access (British, Dutch, French, Portuguese); the transformation from commercial relationship to territorial control; explain European motivations — access to goods (spices, silk, tea, opium), strategic positioning, missionary activity, Enlightenment curiosity; describe the specific mechanism of increasing control in the chosen context (opium trade in China, Company rule in India, Dutch VOC in Indonesia).
wider: Examine the opium trade as a case study in how commercial exploitation could be backed by military force — and what this reveals about the relationship between capitalism and imperialism
Compare the mechanisms of European control in two different Asian societies — examining why different societies experienced different types and intensities of European intervention
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how contact developed from trade to control is the prerequisite for understanding both the effects (N2) and continuity/change analysis (N3). Students who see European domination as sudden cannot explain the differential experiences of Asian societies or the varied responses to contact.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat European colonisation as a sudden imposition rather than as a gradual process with commercial origins. Making the developmental trajectory explicit — trade → commercial dominance → political control — is the scaffold for understanding how the process unfolded and how it could be resisted at different stages.

success_criteria: Describes how European contact with the chosen society developed over time
Identifies at least two European motivations for engagement and explains how each drove increasing contact

nodes.label: Effects of European contact — change and continuity in the chosen society
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify aspects of the chosen Asian society that changed and those that remained the same as a result of European contact.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify at least two changes and at least one continuity in the chosen society resulting from European contact.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe changes — political (loss of sovereignty, new legal systems), economic (integration into European trade systems, deindustrialisation, cash crop monocultures), social (new class structures, missionary influence), cultural (spread of European languages, education systems, religion); and continuities — traditional practices, family structures, religious beliefs, cultural arts that persisted under or alongside colonial rule; apply the continuity-change framework from K05; examine how different social groups experienced contact differently — elites who collaborated, peasants who resisted, artisans displaced by imports.
wider: Examine the British Raj's infrastructure legacy (railways, telegraph, schools, law) and evaluate whether its long-term effects were primarily beneficial or harmful — examining the debate from Indian and British perspectives
Investigate how colonial contact changed gender relations in the chosen society — examining what changed for women specifically and what forces drove those changes

response_modes.reason: Students commonly focus on dramatic political changes (loss of sovereignty) without examining the economic, social and cultural changes that often had greater effects on everyday life. Multiple domains of change — and attention to continuities — build the fuller picture.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two changes resulting from European contact with the chosen society
Identifies at least one significant continuity and explains why it persisted
